contribution: A harmonic force makes a body perform simple harmonic motion: the factors that the period depends on are investigated with a simulation that integrates the motion, and they give the formulas $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\tfrac{m}{k}}$ and, for small swings, $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\tfrac{l}{g}}$, the conservation of energy $E = \tfrac{1}{2}kA^2$ in oscillation, and the measurement of the period of a pendulum with its uncertainty.
learn: recognise simple harmonic motion and explain which quantities affect the period.
calculate the period and the frequency of a mass on a spring and of a pendulum.
determine the period of a pendulum from a measurement, with its uncertainty.
prior: The period $T$ is the duration of one cycle, the frequency is $f = \tfrac{1}{T}$ and the amplitude is the greatest displacement from the equilibrium position (chapter *Describing oscillation: period, frequency and amplitude*)
A harmonic force $F = -kx$ points towards the equilibrium position, and the elastic potential energy of a spring is $\tfrac{1}{2}kx^2$ (chapter *Spring force and spring energy*)

activities.text: In a playground there are two swings side by side with chains of the same length. A small child swings on one and her father on the other. On the edge of the sandpit there is a toy in which a wooden bird bobs up and down on a spring, and the child pulls it a little at one moment and a lot at another. Each of these oscillates back and forth at its own pace.
activities.question: Which quantities determine how long one oscillation back and forth takes, and which do not affect it at all?

activities.title: Recall: the harmonic force
activities.prompt: A body on a frictionless surface is attached to a spring with a spring constant of $40\,\text{N/m}$. The body is pulled $5.0\,\text{cm}$ to the right of the equilibrium position and held still. In which direction does the force of the spring on the body point, and how large is it?

choices.text: To the left, towards the equilibrium position, $2.0\,\text{N}$.
choices.feedback: Correct. The harmonic force is $F = -kx$: its magnitude is $kx = 40\,\text{N/m} \cdot 0.050\,\text{m} = 2.0\,\text{N}$, and the minus sign tells us that it points against the displacement, that is, towards the equilibrium position (chapter *Spring force and spring energy*). Today we find out what kind of motion this force produces when the body is released.

choices.text: To the right, in the direction of the displacement, $2.0\,\text{N}$.
choices.feedback: The magnitude is right, but a stretched spring pulls the body back and does not push it further away. The force of the spring always points towards the equilibrium position, which is why the formula $F = -kx$ has a minus sign.

choices.text: To the left, $200\,\text{N}$.
choices.feedback: The direction is right, but the displacement was substituted in centimetres. The unit of the spring constant is $\text{N/m}$, so the displacement must be converted to metres: $5.0\,\text{cm} = 0.050\,\text{m}$, and the force is $2.0\,\text{N}$.

choices.text: There is no force, because the body is at rest.
choices.feedback: The body is at rest because a hand holds it in place: the force of the hand and the force of the spring cancel each other. A stretched spring pulls the body all the time, and this very force sets it moving when the hand lets go.

activities.title: Prediction 1: a larger oscillation
activities.prompt: A body at the end of a spring is first pulled $5\,\text{cm}$ and then $10\,\text{cm}$ from the equilibrium position and released from rest. The surface is frictionless. How does the period change when the amplitude is doubled?

choices.text: The period increases, because the body has to travel a longer distance.
choices.feedback: The values of the model refute this: the period is $0.993\,\text{s}$ with both the $5\,\text{cm}$ and the $10\,\text{cm}$ amplitude. The distance does double, but so does the greatest speed, from $0.316\,\text{m/s}$ to $0.632\,\text{m/s}$, because farther out the spring pulls with twice the force.

choices.text: The period decreases, because the force of the spring is greater.
choices.feedback: The values of the model refute this: the period stays at $0.993\,\text{s}$. A greater force gives a greater speed, but the body also has to travel twice the distance, and these cancel each other exactly.

choices.text: The period stays the same.
choices.feedback: The values of the model support this: the period is $0.993\,\text{s}$ with both amplitudes. With double the amplitude the spring pulls with double the force at every corresponding point, and the greatest speed doubles to $0.632\,\text{m/s}$. The longer distance is covered at a greater speed in the same time.

activities.title: Prediction 2: a heavier pendulum bob
activities.prompt: The $0.10\,\text{kg}$ bob of a pendulum one metre long is replaced with a $1.0\,\text{kg}$ bob. The length of the string and the small starting angle stay the same, and air resistance is neglected. How does the period of the pendulum change?

choices.text: The period decreases, because a greater weight acts on a heavier bob and pulls it down faster.
choices.feedback: The values of the model refute this: the period is $2.010\,\text{s}$ for all the masses. A greater force acts on a heavier bob, but it is just as much harder to accelerate, so the acceleration $a = \tfrac{F}{m}$ is the same, as in free fall.

choices.text: The period increases, because a heavy bob is slow to start and slow to stop.
choices.feedback: The values of the model refute this: the period stays at $2.010\,\text{s}$. It is true that the inertia is greater, but the restoring force, the component of the weight along the path, also grows with the mass. When both grow tenfold, the acceleration does not change.

choices.text: The period stays the same.
choices.feedback: The values of the model support this: the period is $2.010\,\text{s}$ with both the $0.10\,\text{kg}$ and the $1.0\,\text{kg}$ bob. The weight and the inertia grow in the same proportion, so the acceleration and the whole motion stay the same. Only the energy grows tenfold.

activities.text: Choose an oscillator, adjust its quantities and start it. Use the graph to see how long one cycle takes.
activities.howto: Choose *Oscillator*: a mass on a spring or a pendulum. Use the sliders to set the mass and the spring constant or the length, and the amplitude or the starting angle, and press *Start*. The body starts from rest at an extreme position. The graph plots the position $x$ or the angle $\alpha$ as a function of time, and the label $T$ shows the interval between the two most recent extreme positions on the same side. Above the graph you see the stopwatch time $t$ and the number of complete cycles $n$. The bar under the canvas shows how the energy is divided between kinetic energy $E_\text{k}$ and potential energy $E_\text{p}$. For the spring, the lengths of the arrows are relative to the greatest value of each quantity during the motion; for the pendulum, the arrows are drawn to the same scale in all settings, so in a small swing they are short. *Speed* changes only the pace of the animation, not the period. When you change a value, the body returns to its starting position.
activities.model: The surface of the mass on a spring is frictionless, and the only force along the motion is the harmonic force of the spring, $F = -kx$. The pendulum is a simple pendulum: a point mass on a massless string without air resistance, and its motion is calculated from the exact equation also at large angles, so the small-angle approximation has not been made. There is no damping, so the energy is conserved. The period, the frequency and the energies are values calculated by the model, not measurements.
activities.calc: The motion is calculated in small time steps: at each step the acceleration is obtained from the force ($a = -\tfrac{k}{m}x$ for the spring and the tangential acceleration $a_\text{t} = -g\sin\alpha$ for the pendulum), and the speed and the position are updated from it. The period $T$ is the time measured from the motion, from the starting moment until the body has again stopped at the same extreme position; it is not calculated from the formula for the period. The frequency is $f = \tfrac{1}{T}$. The energy is $E = \tfrac{1}{2}kA^2$ for the spring and $E = mgl(1 - \cos\alpha_0)$ for the pendulum, when the zero level of the potential energy is at the lowest point of the pendulum; $g = 9.81\,\text{m/s}^2$.

activities.title: Experiment 1: only the amplitude changes
activities.intro: Test prediction 1. The mass of the body and the spring constant stay constant; change only the amplitude. Record the period, the greatest speed and the energy with at least the amplitudes $0.05\,\text{m}$ and $0.10\,\text{m}$, and if you like also $0.20\,\text{m}$. Start the oscillator from time to time and see how long a cycle is in the graph.

activities.title: Experiment 2: only the mass changes
activities.intro: The spring constant and the amplitude stay constant; change only the mass of the body. Record the period with at least the masses $0.50\,\text{kg}$ and $2.00\,\text{kg}$, and if you like also $0.20\,\text{kg}$ and $0.80\,\text{kg}$.

question.prompt: In your table the mass quadrupled from $0.50\,\text{kg}$ to $2.00\,\text{kg}$. How did the period change?

choices.text: The period doubled.
choices.feedback: Correct: from $0.993\,\text{s}$ to $1.987\,\text{s}$. The period is proportional to the square root of the mass, and $\sqrt{4} = 2$.

choices.text: The period quadrupled.
choices.feedback: Look at the table again: $0.993\,\text{s}$ changed to $1.987\,\text{s}$, that is, only doubled. The period is not directly proportional to the mass but to its square root.

choices.text: The period halved.
choices.feedback: A greater mass accelerates more slowly under the same force of the spring, so the period increases and does not decrease: from $0.993\,\text{s}$ to $1.987\,\text{s}$.

activities.title: Experiment 3: the mass of the pendulum changes
activities.intro: Test prediction 2. The length of the pendulum is $1.00\,\text{m}$ and the starting angle is $10^\circ$; change only the mass of the bob. Record the period and the energy with at least the masses $0.10\,\text{kg}$ and $1.00\,\text{kg}$.

activities.title: Experiment 4: the length of the pendulum changes
activities.intro: The mass of the bob is $0.50\,\text{kg}$ and the starting angle is $10^\circ$; change only the length of the pendulum. Record the period with at least the lengths $0.25\,\text{m}$ and $1.00\,\text{m}$. By what factor does the period change when the length is quadrupled?

activities.title: Extension: large swings
activities.intro: The length of the pendulum is $1.00\,\text{m}$; change only the starting angle. Record the period with, for example, the angles $5^\circ$, $20^\circ$, $40^\circ$ and $60^\circ$, and compare it with the small-angle value $2\pi\sqrt{\tfrac{l}{g}} = 2.006\,\text{s}$. At what angle does the difference start to show?

question.prompt: What does your table tell you about the period of a pendulum at large starting angles? Why does the period increase at large angles? When can the formula $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\tfrac{l}{g}}$ be used?
question.model: At small angles the period is almost the same: $2.007\,\text{s}$ at $5^\circ$ and $2.010\,\text{s}$ at $10^\circ$, less than $0.2\,\%$ above the value $2.006\,\text{s}$ given by the formula. At large angles the period increases: $2.021\,\text{s}$ at $20^\circ$, $2.069\,\text{s}$ at $40^\circ$ and $2.153\,\text{s}$ at $60^\circ$, about $7\,\%$ above. The restoring force $mg\sin\alpha$ remains smaller at large angles than in the harmonic model, so the pendulum returns more slowly. The formula can be used when the swings are small, below about $10^\circ$. The values are calculated by the model.
criteria: I compared the periods at small and large angles with numbers.
I explained the difference by $\sin\alpha$ being smaller than the angle in radians.
I said that the formula holds for small swings.

activities.title: Conclusion: what does the period depend on?
activities.prompt: Write, on the basis of your tables: which quantities changed the period of the mass on a spring and which did not? What about the pendulum? By what factor did the period change when the mass or the length was quadrupled? Why does the mass matter for the spring but not for the pendulum?
activities.model: The period of the mass on a spring stayed at $0.993\,\text{s}$ when the amplitude increased from $0.05\,\text{m}$ to $0.10\,\text{m}$; the greatest speed doubled and the energy quadrupled. When the mass quadrupled from $0.50\,\text{kg}$ to $2.00\,\text{kg}$, the period doubled to $1.99\,\text{s}$. The period of the pendulum was $2.01\,\text{s}$ for all the masses, but when the length quadrupled from $0.25\,\text{m}$ to $1.00\,\text{m}$, the period doubled from $1.00\,\text{s}$ to $2.01\,\text{s}$. So the period is proportional to the square root of the mass or of the length. For the spring the mass matters because the force of the spring does not grow with the mass; for the pendulum the restoring force is a part of the weight and grows with the mass. The values are calculated by the model, without friction and air resistance.
criteria: I stated with numbers that the amplitude did not change the period of the spring and the mass did not change the period of the pendulum.
I stated that a quadrupled mass (spring) or length (pendulum) doubled the period.
I explained why the mass matters for the spring but not for the pendulum.
I mentioned that the values are model values without friction and air resistance.

activities.title: Return to your predictions
activities.prompt: Compare your predictions with the values of the model in the experiments and with the formulas $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\tfrac{m}{k}}$ and $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\tfrac{l}{g}}$. Then return to the question at the beginning: do the child and her father swing at the same pace if they swing on chains of equal length with small swings? What determines the pace at which the wooden bird bobs?

activities.title: Experimental work: determining the period of a pendulum
activities.text:
A student hung a weight on a thin string so that the length of the pendulum from the point of suspension to the centre of mass of the weight was $1.000\,\text{m}$, and displaced it by about $5^\circ$. With a stopwatch she measured the time of ten complete cycles five times. The watch was started and stopped when the weight passed the equilibrium position moving in the same direction, because at that point the weight moves fastest and the moment of passing can be seen most accurately.

| Measurement | $10T$ (s) |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | $20.12$ |
| 2 | $19.94$ |
| 3 | $20.21$ |
| 4 | $19.88$ |
| 5 | $20.05$ |

The uncertainty of timing by hand is about $0.2\,\text{s}$, even though the watch shows hundredths. When ten cycles are measured, the same uncertainty is divided among ten cycles.

question.prompt: Calculate the period $T$ of the pendulum from the mean of the measurements. Answer in seconds.
hints: The table gives the time of ten cycles. What must you calculate first, and what do you divide it by?
Calculate the mean of the five measurements and divide it by ten.

mistakes.feedback: This is the time of ten cycles. The time of one cycle is obtained by dividing it by ten.
You divided the mean by five, the number of measurements. The number in the table is the time of ten cycles, so it is divided by ten.

question.solution:
**Given:** length of the pendulum $l = 1.000\,\text{m}$, times of ten cycles $20.12\,\text{s}$, $19.94\,\text{s}$, $20.21\,\text{s}$, $19.88\,\text{s}$ and $20.05\,\text{s}$, uncertainty of timing by hand about $0.2\,\text{s}$

**Find:** the period $T$ in $\text{s}$

**Principle:** The mean of repeated measurements reduces the effect of random error. The time of ten cycles is ten times the period, and because the uncertainty of timing concerns only the starting and stopping moments, measuring ten cycles reduces the uncertainty of the period to one tenth.

**Formula:** $\overline{t}_{10} = \dfrac{t_1 + t_2 + t_3 + t_4 + t_5}{5}$ and $T = \dfrac{\overline{t}_{10}}{10}$, $\Delta T = \dfrac{\Delta t}{10}$

**Conversions:** The times are in seconds, so no conversions are needed.

**Substitution:** $\overline{t}_{10} = \dfrac{100.20\,\text{s}}{5} = 20.04\,\text{s}$, $T = \dfrac{20.04\,\text{s}}{10} = 2.004\,\text{s}$ and $\Delta T = \dfrac{0.2\,\text{s}}{10} = 0.02\,\text{s}$

**Answer:** $T = 2.004\,\text{s}$, or with its uncertainty $T = (2.00 \pm 0.02)\,\text{s}$. The uncertainty is hundredths of a second, so the result is given to the accuracy of hundredths.

**Reasonableness:** The small-swing formula gives a period of $2.006\,\text{s}$ for a pendulum one metre long, which is within the uncertainty interval of the measurement. The spread of the measurements is of the same order as the estimated uncertainty: half of the range is $\tfrac{20.21\,\text{s} - 19.88\,\text{s}}{2} \approx 0.17\,\text{s}$.

activities.title: Why ten cycles?
activities.prompt: Another student measures the time of one cycle of the same pendulum. Her timing uncertainty is also about $0.2\,\text{s}$. How large is the uncertainty of her period compared with the ten-cycle measurement?

choices.text: About $0.2\,\text{s}$, that is, ten times as large.
choices.feedback: Correct. The uncertainty of timing comes from starting and stopping the watch, not from the number of cycles. In a one-cycle measurement the whole $0.2\,\text{s}$ falls on one cycle, which is about $10\,\%$ of a period of two seconds. In a ten-cycle measurement it is divided among ten cycles.

choices.text: The same $0.02\,\text{s}$, because the watch and the person measuring are the same.
choices.feedback: The same person makes the same timing error of about $0.2\,\text{s}$ in both the one-cycle and the ten-cycle measurement. In the ten-cycle measurement the error is divided by ten, in the one-cycle measurement it is not, so the uncertainty of one cycle is about $0.2\,\text{s}$.

choices.text: About $0.01\,\text{s}$, because the watch shows hundredths of a second.
choices.feedback: The resolution of the watch is $0.01\,\text{s}$, but in timing by hand the reaction time is a much greater source of uncertainty. The uncertainty can be greater than the smallest scale division: about $0.2\,\text{s}$ per measurement.

choices.text: About $2\,\text{s}$, that is, a hundred times as large.
choices.feedback: The uncertainty does not grow when fewer cycles are measured: in a one-cycle measurement the timing uncertainty of about $0.2\,\text{s}$ falls directly on the period. In a ten-cycle measurement it is reduced to one tenth per cycle.

activities.title: The acceleration of free fall from a pendulum
activities.prompt: Calculate the acceleration of free fall $g$ from the period $T = 2.004\,\text{s}$ and the length $l = 1.000\,\text{m}$ of the previous measurement. The swings were small. Answer in $\text{m/s}^2$.
hints: Which formula for the period do you use, and which quantity in it must now be solved?

mistakes.feedback: You substituted the time of ten cycles, $20.04\,\text{s}$, as the period. The formula needs the time of one cycle, $2.004\,\text{s}$.
The period is in the denominator of the formula squared: $g = \tfrac{4\pi^2 l}{T^2}$.

activities.solution:
**Given:** length of the pendulum $l = 1.000\,\text{m}$, period $T = (2.004 \pm 0.02)\,\text{s}$, small swings

**Find:** the acceleration of free fall $g$ in $\text{m/s}^2$

**Principle:** For small swings the period of a pendulum depends only on the length and the acceleration of free fall, so when the length and the period have been measured, the acceleration of free fall can be solved. A starting angle of about $5^\circ$ is so small that the error of the small-angle formula is below $0.1\,\%$.

**Formula:** $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g}}$, so $T^2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2 l}{g}$ and $g = \dfrac{4\pi^2 l}{T^2}$

**Conversions:** The length is in metres and the time in seconds, so no conversions are needed.

**Substitution:** $g = \dfrac{4\pi^2 \cdot 1.000\,\text{m}}{(2.004\,\text{s})^2} = \dfrac{39.48\,\text{m}}{4.016\,\text{s}^2} = 9.830\,\text{m/s}^2$

**Answer:** $g \approx 9.8\,\text{m/s}^2$. The uncertainty of the period is about $1\,\%$, and because $T$ is squared in the formula, the uncertainty of $g$ is about $2\,\%$: with $T = 2.024\,\text{s}$ and $T = 1.984\,\text{s}$ we get $9.64\,\text{m/s}^2$ and $10.03\,\text{m/s}^2$. The result is therefore given to two significant figures, $g = (9.8 \pm 0.2)\,\text{m/s}^2$.

**Reasonableness:** The table value $9.81\,\text{m/s}^2$ is within the uncertainty interval. A more accurate result is obtained by measuring the period with several lengths and determining the acceleration of free fall from the slope of the $(l, T^2)$ graph; that is done in the investigation *Determining the acceleration of free fall with a pendulum*.

activities.title: Find the error
activities.prompt:
A student calculates the period of a $0.80\,\text{m}$ pendulum like this:

$$\begin{aligned} T &= 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{g}{l}} \\ &= 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{9.81}{0.80}}\,\text{s} \\ &\approx 22\,\text{s} \end{aligned}$$

Where is the error?

choices.text: The length and the acceleration of free fall have changed places in the formula.
choices.feedback: Correct: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\tfrac{l}{g}} \approx 1.79\,\text{s}$. The error could have been noticed from the units: $\sqrt{\tfrac{\text{m/s}^2}{\text{m}}} = \tfrac{1}{\text{s}}$, which is not a unit of time. Experience helps too: a pendulum shorter than a metre swings in about two seconds, not in $22\,\text{s}$.

choices.text: The length should have been converted to centimetres.
choices.feedback: The formula uses SI units, so the length is right in metres. The error is in the formula itself: substitute the units and you will see that the result is not in seconds.

choices.text: The mass of the pendulum is missing from the formula.
choices.feedback: The period of a simple pendulum does not depend on the mass: the weight and the inertia grow in the same proportion, and the mass cancels. The error is that $l$ and $g$ have changed places.

choices.text: The angle should have been taken into account, because the pendulum swings.
choices.feedback: For small swings the angle does not affect the period significantly, and the pendulum of the task swings normally. The error is bigger: $l$ and $g$ have changed places, which shows in the units.

activities.title: Apply to a new situation
activities.prompt: On a space station scales do not work, because everything is weightless. The mass of an astronaut is therefore measured with a chair that oscillates on a spring. The mass of the chair itself is $10.0\,\text{kg}$ and the spring constant of the spring is $1200\,\text{N/m}$. When the astronaut sits in the chair, ten cycles take $16.6\,\text{s}$. What is the mass of the astronaut? Answer in kilograms.
hints: Why does the period of a spring work in weightlessness too, even though weight does not? Which quantity in the formula for the period is unknown?
First calculate $T$ from the time of ten cycles, and solve the total oscillating mass from the formula $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\tfrac{m}{k}}$: $m = \tfrac{kT^2}{4\pi^2}$.
The total mass is $\dfrac{1200\,\text{N/m} \cdot (1.66\,\text{s})^2}{4\pi^2} \approx 83.8\,\text{kg}$. What must still be subtracted from it?

mistakes.feedback: This is the combined mass of the chair and the astronaut. The chair oscillates on the spring too, so its mass $10.0\,\text{kg}$ must be subtracted.
You used the time of ten cycles, $16.6\,\text{s}$, as the period. The time of one cycle is $1.66\,\text{s}$.
The period is squared in the formula $m = \tfrac{kT^2}{4\pi^2}$.

activities.solution:
**Given:** mass of the chair $m_\text{c} = 10.0\,\text{kg}$, spring constant $k = 1200\,\text{N/m}$, time of ten cycles $t = 16.6\,\text{s}$

**Find:** the mass of the astronaut $m_\text{a}$ in $\text{kg}$

**Principle:** The period of a mass on a spring depends on the mass, that is, the inertia, and not on the weight, so the measurement works in weightlessness. The chair and the astronaut oscillate together on the spring, and the only force along the motion is the harmonic force of the spring.

**Formula:** $T = \dfrac{t}{10}$ and $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m_\text{c} + m_\text{a}}{k}}$, so $m_\text{c} + m_\text{a} = \dfrac{kT^2}{4\pi^2}$ and $m_\text{a} = \dfrac{kT^2}{4\pi^2} - m_\text{c}$

**Conversions:** The quantities are in SI units, so no conversions are needed.

**Substitution:** $T = \dfrac{16.6\,\text{s}}{10} = 1.66\,\text{s}$ and $m_\text{a} = \dfrac{1200\,\text{N/m} \cdot (1.66\,\text{s})^2}{4\pi^2} - 10.0\,\text{kg} = 83.76\,\text{kg} - 10.0\,\text{kg} = 73.76\,\text{kg}$

**Answer:** $73.8\,\text{kg}$, three significant figures as in the time $16.6\,\text{s}$.

**Reasonableness:** The mass of an adult is typically $60$–$90\,\text{kg}$, so the result is believable. Check: with the total mass $83.76\,\text{kg}$ the formula gives a period of $1.66\,\text{s}$. A heavier astronaut would make the chair oscillate more slowly.

activities.text: Practise at three levels. Level 1 tasks use one formula, in level 2 tasks another quantity is solved from the formula or two situations are compared, and level 3 combines two ideas.

activities.title: 1. Concept
activities.prompt: A mass oscillating on a spring and a pendulum one metre long are taken from the Earth to the Moon, where the acceleration of free fall is about one sixth of the value on the Earth. The swings are small. How do their periods change?

choices.text: The period of the spring stays the same, the period of the pendulum increases.
choices.feedback: Correct. The period of the spring, $2\pi\sqrt{\tfrac{m}{k}}$, depends on the mass and the spring constant, which are the same on the Moon. The restoring force of the pendulum is a part of the weight, which is smaller on the Moon, so the period $2\pi\sqrt{\tfrac{l}{g}}$ increases by a factor of about $\sqrt{6} \approx 2.4$.

choices.text: Both periods increase, because everything is lighter on the Moon.
choices.feedback: The mass of a body does not change on the Moon, only its weight. The period of the spring depends on the mass and the spring constant, so it stays the same. The period of the pendulum increases, because its restoring force is a part of the weight.

choices.text: Both periods stay the same, because the masses do not change.
choices.feedback: This is true for the spring, but the restoring force of the pendulum is a component of the weight. On the Moon the weight is smaller, so the pendulum returns to the equilibrium position more slowly and its period increases.

choices.text: The period of the pendulum stays the same, the period of the spring increases.
choices.feedback: It is the other way round. The period of the pendulum, $2\pi\sqrt{\tfrac{l}{g}}$, depends on the acceleration of free fall; the period of the spring, $2\pi\sqrt{\tfrac{m}{k}}$, does not.

activities.title: 2. From a graph to the spring constant
activities.prompt: The graph shows the position of a $0.25\,\text{kg}$ body oscillating without friction on a spring. Determine the period from the graph and calculate the spring constant of the spring. Answer in $\text{N/m}$.
hints: Where in the graph is the period read? Find two successive peaks.
The peaks are at the times $0\,\text{s}$ and $0.40\,\text{s}$. Solve $k$ from the formula $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\tfrac{m}{k}}$.

mistakes.feedback: You read the period as $0.20\,\text{s}$, the interval between a peak and a trough. That is half a cycle: a whole cycle is the interval between two successive peaks, $0.40\,\text{s}$.
The period is squared in the formula $k = \tfrac{4\pi^2 m}{T^2}$.

activities.solution:
**Given:** mass $m = 0.25\,\text{kg}$, frictionless oscillation; the period $T$ from the graph

**Find:** the spring constant $k$ in $\text{N/m}$

**Principle:** The only force along the motion is the harmonic force of the spring, so the period is $2\pi\sqrt{\tfrac{m}{k}}$. When the period is read from the graph, the spring constant can be solved.

**Reading the graph:** The peaks of the curve, $x = 3.0\,\text{cm}$, are at the times $0\,\text{s}$, $0.40\,\text{s}$ and $0.80\,\text{s}$. The interval between two successive peaks is one cycle, so $T = 0.40\,\text{s}$. The interval of two cycles divided by two, $0.80\,\text{s} : 2 = 0.40\,\text{s}$, confirms the reading. The amplitude $3.0\,\text{cm}$ is not needed, because the period does not depend on it.

**Formula:** $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}$, so $T^2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2 m}{k}$ and $k = \dfrac{4\pi^2 m}{T^2}$

**Conversions:** The mass is in kilograms and the time in seconds, so no conversions are needed.

**Substitution:** $k = \dfrac{4\pi^2 \cdot 0.25\,\text{kg}}{(0.40\,\text{s})^2} = \dfrac{9.870\,\text{kg}}{0.16\,\text{s}^2} = 61.69\,\text{N/m}$

**Answer:** $62\,\text{N/m}$, two significant figures as in the mass $0.25\,\text{kg}$ and the period $0.40\,\text{s}$.

**Reasonableness:** The frequency is $\tfrac{1}{0.40\,\text{s}} = 2.5\,\text{Hz}$, so a light body on a fairly stiff spring oscillates quickly. Check: with the spring constant $62\,\text{N/m}$ the formula gives a period of about $0.40\,\text{s}$.

activities.title: 3. Explain with energy
activities.prompt: A body at the end of a spring oscillates without friction. Using conservation of energy, explain where the speed of the body is greatest, why doubling the amplitude doubles the greatest speed, and what this tells us about the period.
activities.model: In frictionless oscillation the mechanical energy is conserved: $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}kx^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}kA^2$. The elastic potential energy of the spring is zero at the equilibrium position $x = 0$, so there all the energy is kinetic energy and the speed is greatest. At the extreme positions the speed is zero. For the greatest speed we get $\tfrac{1}{2}mv_\text{max}^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}kA^2$, that is, $v_\text{max} = A\sqrt{\tfrac{k}{m}}$, so it is directly proportional to the amplitude. Doubling the amplitude quadruples the energy, and because the kinetic energy is proportional to the square of the speed, the speed doubles. That is why double the distance is covered in the same period.
criteria: I name the equilibrium position as the point where the speed is greatest and justify it by the elastic potential energy of the spring being zero there.
I write the equation of conservation of energy or its equivalent in words.
I conclude that the energy quadruples but the speed only doubles, because the kinetic energy is proportional to the square of the speed.
I connect the result to the period not depending on the amplitude.

activities.text: Finally, two quick questions. Answer first yourself and only then open the answer.
